title: Six volumes, 1909
hookLine: The Sikh Religion was checked by Sikh scholars before it was published

cards: Before a word went to the printer, it went to the scholars. That was the method Macauliffe describes. He could have trusted his own ear; he'd lived with the hymns for years by then.
Instead, he did something slower and humbler. He showed his English to learned Sikhs, let them argue with it, and changed it when they found a mistake.
The result came out in six volumes, under the plain title The Sikh Religion.

teach.b: First, what the volumes hold. The full title names three things: the Gurus, the sacred writings, and the authors. So it isn't a bare translation.

It tells the lives of the Gurus and the Bhagats, the saints whose hymns sit in the Granth, and sets their verses into that story. A reader meets Guru Nanak's words inside Guru Nanak's life. Second, the checking.
Macauliffe himself describes submitting his translations to Sikh scholars and gyanis, the learned readers of the scripture, and asking for their corrections.
A translation the community's own experts had read and challenged was a different thing from one an outsider had simply guessed at. Third, why that mattered then.
In the reform years, Sikhs were working hard to say clearly who they were. A book in English, read by officials and scholars far beyond the Punjab, could either help or hurt.
Checked this way, it put a Sikh reading of the Sikh faith in front of English readers.

teach.h: THE TRUE THING OVER THE COMFORTABLE.
teach.b: Fourth, the true thing over the comfortable one. The Gurus ask for the truth to be lived, not just spoken.
In Japji, Guru Nanak asks how a person becomes truthful, and answers that it comes through walking in the Lord's will.
Checking your work with someone who knows more is a small way of choosing the true thing over the comfortable one. It costs pride. It saves mistakes that could outlast you.

how: Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion is still read by students of Sikh history and scripture, and because it is now in the public domain, its English renderings of the Gurus' hymns are freely quoted and shared.

games.q: you're Macauliffe. years of work are finished, and the printer is waiting. what do you do with the manuscript?
o: send it straight to print; you know the hymns well by now.
show it to Sikh scholars and change what they correct.

practice: Bring to mind one piece of your own work that matters, a report, a plan, a letter, a way you've been reading a situation at home, and notice where you've been relying on your own guess.
Picture handing it to someone who knows that ground better, notice what that feels like in your chest, and breathe through it. If you pray, let Waheguru steady each breath out.
